strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: reducing the training cost of motion-forecasting models while improving representation of rare, dense-traffic scenes.

The evaluation covers three forecasting configurations—HiVT-64, HiVT-128, and HPNet—and retention ratios from 50% to 1%, providing useful evidence about how performance degrades under increasing compression.

Evaluation on validation subsets with more than 40, 60, and 80 agents is informative. In particular, balanced selection consistently improves over random sampling in dense scenes; for HiVT-64 on the >60-agent subset at 40% retention, minADE improves from 1.292 to 1.216.

The basic idea of combining within-bin selection with density-aware budget allocation is simple, potentially useful, and appears transferable from the HiVT-64 selection backbone to other architectures.
weaknesses: The central coreset objective is not mathematically well defined. Equation (1) defines P(S_j) for an individual sample while implicitly depending on C, whereas Algorithm 1 requires a set function P(C) to compute P(C∪{S_j})−P(C). No set-level definition or proof of submodularity is provided, so the claimed greedy submodular optimization cannot be reconstructed or technically validated.

The interpretation of Equation (1) contradicts its mathematics. Squared differences are described as similarity, although larger values mean greater dissimilarity. Maximizing the first term favors candidates far from the selected set, while subtracting the second favors candidates close to the unselected set—the opposite of parts of the accompanying explanation. This is a material correctness issue rather than a presentation refinement.

The experimental comparisons cannot establish the claimed state-of-the-art compression ratio or the benefit of the proposed scoring function. Random sampling is the only selection baseline; established coreset, importance-sampling, gradient-based, facility-location, and simple agent-count-stratified baselines are absent. There is also no ablation separating density rebalancing from the proposed submodular score.

The efficiency claim is insufficiently supported. Selection requires pretraining HiVT-64 on the full dataset for 10 epochs and apparently evaluating pairwise loss differences during iterative greedy selection, but selection complexity, runtime, memory, and end-to-end GPU-hour savings are not reported. It is therefore unclear whether the approach reduces total computational cost rather than only the subsequent training-set size.

The distribution analysis in Table III is internally unclear. The full-data percentages sum to about 92% because scenes with fewer than 10 agents are omitted, whereas the random and balanced rows approximately sum to 100%; nevertheless, all are compared using a fixed mean of 10%. Moreover, the table aggregates several of the ten stated difficulty levels into a single 60+ column. These inconsistent denominators and aggregation make the reported variance values—and hence a principal balancing claim—difficult to interpret.

Agent count is assumed to represent scenario difficulty without validating that assumption against prediction error or interaction complexity. Dense scenes can contain irrelevant or stationary agents, while sparse scenes can contain difficult interactions. The unspecified removal of infrequently observed agents further changes this quantity.

Reproducibility is limited by missing filtering thresholds, an ambiguous definition of the per-sample objective f, unspecified rounding and tie handling in DynamicBudget, unclear initialization when retraining on a coreset, and no random seeds, repeated trials, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests. Evaluation is also restricted to one older dataset and its validation split.

The claim of strong generalization is overstated: transfer of a selected subset across three architectures on the same dataset demonstrates some model transferability, not generalization across datasets, geographic domains, or distribution shifts. Overall, the promising empirical trend does not outweigh the undefined core objective and insufficient evidence isolating the proposed contribution.

The experiments cover three predictors (HiVT-64, HiVT-128, and HPNet), several retention ratios, and validation subsets stratified by agent count. Transferring a coreset constructed with HiVT-64 to the other architectures is a useful experimental direction.

The reported results suggest that density-aware sampling can help on dense subsets. For example, with HiVT-64 and 40% retention on scenes containing more than 60 agents, balanced selection obtains 1.216 minADE versus 1.292 for random sampling.
weaknesses: The core method is not technically well-defined. Equation (1) defines P(S_j), although Algorithm 1 requires a set function P(C) to compute marginal gains P(C union {S_j})-P(C). Moreover, squared loss differences are described as similarity even though larger values indicate dissimilarity. The stated maximization favors candidates far from selected samples while close to unselected samples, and no proof is given that the stated quantity is submodular. Consequently, the algorithm cannot be reproduced unambiguously and the claimed submodular justification is unsupported.

Algorithm 1's balanced-budget bookkeeping appears inconsistent with a fixed global retention ratio. It resets the budget to alpha times the currently remaining dataset at every difficulty level; after fully selecting a rare class, this generally produces a total different from alpha times the original dataset. Integer handling and the precise relationship between the algorithm's classes and the experimental bins are also unspecified.

The claimed computational advantage is not established. Selection requires pretraining HiVT-64 on the complete dataset for 10 epochs and seemingly evaluating pairwise loss differences over a dataset of approximately 206,000 scenes. The paper reports neither selection complexity, runtime, memory, nor end-to-end GPU-hour savings, so it is unclear whether this procedure reduces total computation.

The empirical comparison is inadequate for the main coreset claim. Despite discussing numerous coreset techniques, the only experimental baseline is random sampling; there are no comparisons with facility-location, gradient-matching, uncertainty, diversity, or simpler density-stratified sampling. Thus, the results cannot show that the proposed loss-based selection contributes beyond oversampling dense scenes, nor support the claimed state-of-the-art compression ratio.

The statistical evidence is weak: results are reported without repeated runs, error bars, or significance tests, even where differences are only a few hundredths. The sizes of the greater-than-40, greater-than-60, and greater-than-80 validation subsets are omitted, making the reliability of dense-scene results impossible to judge.

The data-distribution analysis contains unresolved inconsistencies. The displayed full-dataset percentages sum to 92% because scenes with fewer than 10 agents are omitted, whereas other rows are apparently normalized to approximately 100%. A random half-sample of roughly 100,000 scenes also shifts markedly from the stated full distribution, which is implausible without a different denominator or sampling procedure. The text alternately describes ten difficulty levels while Table III reports six aggregated groups, leaving the variance calculation unclear.

Agent count is treated as a direct proxy for prediction difficulty without validation. No analysis controls for relevant alternatives such as interaction intensity, agent type, visibility, map complexity, or target motion, so the broader claim of reducing bias toward easy scenarios is stronger than the evidence supports.

Evaluation is confined to Argoverse 1.1 and in-distribution validation splits. Cross-architecture transfer is useful, but it does not establish the claimed generalization across datasets or domains. Important reproducibility details—including the filtering threshold, exact class boundaries, per-sample loss computation, checkpoints, seeds, and implementation availability—are missing. These issues, combined with the undefined central objective, are consequential rather than presentational and favor rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: reducing the substantial data and training costs of motion-forecasting systems while improving coverage of underrepresented dense-traffic scenes.
The fixed and balanced strategies are intuitive, and evaluating retention ratios from 1% to 50% provides useful evidence about degradation under aggressive compression.

The experiments cover HiVT-64, HiVT-128, and HPNet, suggesting some cross-architecture transfer. On scenes with more than 60 agents, the balanced 40% subset improves HiVT-64 minADE from 1.292 for random selection to 1.216, even slightly outperforming the 1.248 full-data result. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/690b11214b9d462e87f594cbbb179720/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The manuscript reports all three standard forecasting metrics and separately analyzes increasingly dense validation subsets, which is more informative than reporting aggregate accuracy alone.
weaknesses: The central mathematical formulation is not technically sound as written. Equation (1) defines P(S_j) using the current selected set C, whereas Algorithm 1 requires a set function P(C) to compute a marginal gain. If Equation (1) is interpreted as the marginal itself, adding an element k to C increases the marginal of j by 2|f(S_k)-f(S_j)|^2, exhibiting increasing rather than diminishing returns. Thus the claimed submodularity and associated greedy justification do not follow. The text also calls squared differences a similarity while maximizing them in the first term, further obscuring what the criterion optimizes.

The claimed computational efficiency is not established. Selection first requires training HiVT-64 on the complete dataset for 10 epochs and then repeatedly scoring candidates in a greedy loop. No complexity analysis, selection runtime, memory consumption, end-to-end GPU-hour comparison, or approximation strategy is reported; a literal implementation appears potentially quadratic and may offset the downstream training savings.

The main comparisons are only against random sampling. Established subset-selection baselines such as uncertainty/entropy selection, forgetting or EL2N-style scores, gradient matching, facility-location methods, and simpler agent-count-stratified sampling are absent. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate whether gains come from the proposed score, from oversampling dense scenes, or merely from stratification.

The data-distribution analysis is internally inconsistent. The full-data percentages shown in Table III total only about 92% because scenes with fewer than 10 agents are excluded, yet the calculation fixes the category mean at 10% as though the included mass totaled 100%. The paper also describes ten difficulty levels while the table aggregates them into six columns. This makes the reported variance values difficult to interpret or reproduce and weakens the evidence for improved balance.

Several implementation details needed for reproducibility are unspecified: the threshold for removing agents that appear 'infrequently,' the exact per-sample definition and evaluation checkpoint of f, integer handling and total-budget guarantees in DynamicBudget, whether subset models are initialized from scratch, and whether filtering changes the denominator of the reported retention ratios.

The evidence is limited to one older dataset and apparently one run per setting, without error bars or significance tests. Agent count is assumed to measure scenario difficulty but is not validated against prediction error, interaction intensity, or safety-critical events. Evaluation on only dense subsets can also favor the balanced sampler by construction, so aggregate and per-bin tradeoffs require clearer analysis.

Overall, the empirical trend is promising, but the undefined/inconsistent objective, absence of competitive selection baselines, and lack of end-to-end efficiency evidence are material weaknesses rather than presentation refinements. They prevent the current manuscript from adequately supporting its principal technical and practical claims.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: reducing the substantial data and training costs of motion forecasting while improving coverage of underrepresented dense scenes.

Evaluation spans Argoverse 1 and 2 and four forecasting architectures. Cross-architecture transfer—selecting with HiVT/QCNet and training HPNet/DeMo—provides useful evidence that the subsets are not entirely backbone-specific.

Reported results are consistently stronger than random, k-means, and herding selection. On Argoverse 1, 50% SSTP data yields HiVT-64 minADE 0.704 versus 0.695 with all data and 0.750 with random selection; the largest benefits appear in high-density scenes.
The partitioning and submodular components are separately ablated, and sensitivity to retention ratio, pretraining duration, partition interval, and selection backbone is examined.
weaknesses: The method is not technically specified well enough to verify. Equation 4 takes an elementwise product between a gradient with respect to predicted trajectories and a decoder latent vector without defining compatible dimensions; moreover, the classification loss is described as operating on mode probabilities, making its gradient with respect to trajectory coordinates unclear.

The claimed submodular formulation is incomplete. Equation 5 defines a sample-dependent score rather than a set function, and no derivation, submodularity proof, monotonicity condition, or approximation guarantee is given. Its naive evaluation also appears quadratic, but computational implementation and complexity are omitted.

Algorithm 1 seemingly fails to subtract fully included high-density partitions from the remaining budget because the budget update is inside the alternative branch. As written, the output can exceed the stated retention budget. This is a material correctness and reproducibility issue.

Evidence for safety-critical and high-density improvements is insufficiently reliable: Table 4 gives no sample counts or uncertainty, uses overlapping thresholds, reports only one model/dataset despite broader textual claims, and no experiments report multiple runs, standard deviations, or significance. This matters because several overall differences are small.

Baseline coverage is weak for a coreset paper. The evaluation omits stronger gradient-based or submodular selectors, including the cited Grad-Match family, so it does not establish whether the gains arise from the proposed gradient criterion rather than density-stratified sampling with a stronger standard selector.

There are troubling experimental inconsistencies. A uniform random 50% subset should approximately preserve the full dataset's 93.88/6.12 density split, yet Table 5 reports 85.16/14.84 without explanation. HPNet full-training time is variously reported as 256, 268.8, and 307.2 hours, and the end-to-end HiVT saving is only 7.78 to 6.37 hours after selection overhead.

Reproducibility is poor: the code link is an empty GitHub URL, while the selected decoder layer, gradient aggregation, normalization, default partition interval, random seeds, baseline configurations, and efficient implementation of the greedy selection are not documented.

The core idea—density-stratified quotas combined with gradient/similarity-based coreset selection—is potentially useful but largely adapts established coreset mechanisms. Given the unresolved formulation and evidence issues, the empirical contribution does not yet outweigh the technical uncertainty.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: reducing the substantial training cost of motion-forecasting models while improving coverage of underrepresented, dense traffic scenes.

The evaluation spans two established datasets and four prediction architectures. In particular, subsets selected with HiVT or QCNet are also evaluated with other models, providing some evidence of cross-architecture transfer.

Across the reported retention ratios, SSTP consistently outperforms random selection, clustering, and herding. At 50% retention on Argoverse 1, it remains reasonably close to full-data training across HiVT-64, HiVT-128, and HPNet.
The density-stratified results are potentially useful: on the reported HiVT experiment, SSTP improves all three metrics over full-data training for scenes containing at least 60 or 80 agents.
Ablations separately examine density partitioning, the similarity-based selector, pretraining duration, retention ratio, selection backbone, and partition interval.
weaknesses: The central method is not technically established as claimed. Equation 5 defines a candidate-dependent score rather than a set function, and the paper neither identifies an underlying submodular objective nor proves submodularity or a greedy approximation property. Consequently, statements that the procedure 'optimally represents' the dataset are unsupported.

Algorithm 1 appears internally incorrect: when an entire density partition is included at lines 7–8, its size is not deducted from the remaining budget because the budget update is inside the alternative branch. As written, the output can exceed the specified retention budget. This is material to correctness and reproducibility, not merely presentation.

The gradient representation is underspecified and potentially dimensionally inconsistent: an output-trajectory gradient is element-wise multiplied by a decoder latent vector without defining their shapes, alignment across agents/modes/timesteps, aggregation, or the exact layer used. The implementation URL is only a placeholder, so the method cannot be reliably reproduced from the manuscript.

The empirical comparisons are not strong enough to isolate the claimed contribution. Despite citing gradient-based coreset literature, the paper compares only with random selection, k-means, and herding. It omits relevant modern selection methods such as GradMatch and lacks the especially important control of random sampling under exactly the same density quotas. Thus it is unclear how much is gained by the proposed score beyond simple density rebalancing.

No results include repeated runs, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Many central differences are small—for example, the full-versus-50%-subset gaps on Argoverse 1—so claims of significant, robust, or nearly identical performance cannot be assessed against training variance.

Evidence for the safety-critical and long-tail claims is limited. Agent count is used as the sole proxy for scenario difficulty, the nested high-density groups have no reported sample counts, and the principal density table reports only one model/dataset despite the text claiming corresponding results for HPNet and Argoverse 2. Dense scenes are not necessarily rare or safety-critical in the behavioral sense.

The efficiency claim is overstated and incompletely accounted for. For HiVT, the reported end-to-end cost is 6.37 hours versus 7.78 hours, only about an 18% reduction despite retaining 50% of the data. Selection costs for the other dataset/model settings are absent, and HPNet training times are inconsistent between Figure 1 and the main text (268.8 versus 307.2 hours). Memory use and the potentially large pairwise-similarity cost are also unreported.

Several inconsistencies weaken confidence in the experimental record: full-data HiVT metrics differ between Tables 2 and 5 without explanation; Table 4's accompanying prose refers to experiments not present in the table; and broad claims of model independence and cross-dataset generalization rest on only two selector backbones and no transfer of a subset or selection rule across datasets.

The combination of density stratification, gradient-derived features, and greedy similarity selection is sensible but appears incremental relative to established stratified sampling and coreset selection. Given the unresolved objective, limited baselines, and missing uncertainty analysis, the current evidence does not establish sufficient originality or reliability for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: reducing the substantial training cost of motion-forecasting models while improving coverage of underrepresented, high-density traffic scenes.

The empirical evidence is reasonably broad. SSTP is evaluated on Argoverse 1 and Argoverse 2, with subsets transferred across five model configurations spanning HiVT, HPNet, QCNet, and DeMo. Across 40–60% retention, it consistently outperforms random, clustering, and herding selection.

The high-density analysis provides evidence beyond aggregate benchmark metrics. With 50% of Argoverse 1, SSTP improves the full-data model for scenes containing at least 60 agents and produces particularly large gains for at least 80 agents, while incurring only modest degradation in low-density scenes.

Ablations separately examine density partitioning, gradient-based selection, retention ratio, pretraining duration, partition interval, and selection backbone. Table 5 supports the claim that partitioning and the proposed selection rule provide complementary benefits.

The method is conceptually simple and potentially useful: selection is performed once, and subsets selected with one architecture remain effective for other architectures. The reported end-to-end training-time reductions further establish practical value.
weaknesses: Material technical concern: the manuscript calls P a submodular gain function, but Eq. 5 defines a candidate-dependent score rather than a set function, and provides neither a proof of submodularity nor an approximation guarantee for the minimization procedure. Consequently, the theoretical characterization of the selection algorithm is unsupported.

Material reproducibility concern: the gradient feature in Eq. 4 is under-specified. The gradient with respect to predicted trajectories and the decoder latent generally have different shapes, yet their element-wise product is not explained. The manuscript also omits how modes, agents, timesteps, and latent dimensions are aggregated into a fixed-length sample vector.

The computational procedure is insufficiently documented. Direct evaluation of Eq. 5 during every greedy iteration appears potentially quadratic or worse in each partition, but no complexity analysis, batching or approximation strategy, memory requirement, or detailed breakdown of pretraining versus gradient extraction versus greedy selection is provided.

The statistical evidence is limited to single reported values: there are no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. This matters because several differences between configurations are only 0.001–0.01.

There are unexplained numerical inconsistencies. For example, Table 5 reports different full-data and random-selection results from Table 2, and its purported random 50% subset changes the proportion of scenes with at least 40 agents from 6.12% to 14.84%. A uniform random subset of this large dataset should approximately preserve that distribution, so the baseline construction or table labeling requires clarification.

The comparison set omits stronger, directly relevant gradient-based coreset methods such as GradMatch, despite citing them. Comparisons only against random, k-means, and herding make it difficult to isolate whether the proposed selection score advances over established deep-data-selection techniques.

Some claims are overstated. Selecting a separate subset on each dataset does not demonstrate cross-dataset generalization, and the HiVT end-to-end saving is 7.78 to 6.37 hours once the 2.17-hour selection cost is included—useful, but less dramatic than the repeated efficiency language suggests. HPNet training times are also inconsistent across Table 1, Figure 1, and Section 4.4.

The motivation equates agent count with scenario difficulty and safety criticality. Density is a useful proxy, but the evaluation does not cover other rare and safety-relevant factors such as unusual maneuvers, map topology, interaction type, or vulnerable road users. This limits the broader claim of balancing diverse or safety-critical scenarios.
